title: The kibbutz
hookLine: collective farms built on shared work

cards: A long dining hall at dusk. Rows of tables, the same plates, the same bread, a hum of people who have worked the same fields since sunrise. Nobody pays at the door.
Nobody gets a bill. The person who drove the tractor today might be serving soup tomorrow. On the wall, a notice for the evening meeting, where everyone gets a vote.
This is a kibbutz, and for the young people who built the early ones, this room was the point.

teach.b: Kibbutz is a Hebrew word for a gathering, a group. It shares its root with the word the Torah uses when it promises that God will gather the scattered people back from among the nations.
The kibbutz took that old verb and made it a farm. The idea was simple and radical. Members held their property and their earnings in common, not as separate families.
They shared the work, and jobs often rotated, so nobody was only ever the boss or only ever the dishwasher.
Big decisions went to the general meeting, where every member had a voice. Money, clothes, sometimes even the raising of children were arranged in common.
The founders of the early ones came out of the labor Zionism of two lessons ago: young people who believed that working the soil with their own hands would heal something in them and in their people.
There were also religious kibbutzim, where members shared the work and also kept Shabbat and prayed together. Life was hard: swamps, heat, sickness, arguments.
And the kibbutz has changed; some now pay members different salaries and run factories as well as farms, and older members sometimes argue about whether that was wise. But the picture stays.

teach.h: GOOD AND PLEASANT, AND ALSO WORK.
teach.b: The psalm puts it in one line, and a song built on it is still sung at Jewish gatherings: "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!" The psalm calls it good and pleasant.
The kibbutz found out it was also work.

how: Kibbutz members have traditionally shared work, meals and decisions through a general meeting; some kibbutzim are religious and keep Shabbat together, and some have changed their economic arrangements over time.

games.q: you have just joined an early kibbutz. tomorrow it's your turn to wash dishes in the dining hall, and you hate washing dishes. what happens?
o: you pay someone else to do it.
you do it; the jobs rotate.
games.why: there was no owner and no pay. work was shared and often rotated, and complaints went to the general meeting.

practice: Find one thing you usually keep for yourself, a meal, a car ride, a skill, an hour, a good book, and picture one person who could use it, or simply enjoy it with you.
See yourself offering it, and notice whether it feels like losing something, gaining something, or both.

wordCard.voice: Kibbutz. A gathering, a group: a community that shared its work, its table and its decisions, sometimes secular, sometimes religious. Today's word.

orig.note: kibbutz: a gathering, a group, from the Hebrew root for gathering.

carryVoice: Your line: together. An old word for gathering, made into a way of life. Until tomorrow.
